extracted.intended_audience: policy officers and secretariats preparing Regulation Impact Statements (RISs) for Ministers’ Meetings, National Standard Setting Bodies and other intergovernmental decision‑making bodies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing consultation and decision-stage Regulation Impact Statements (RISs) to inform Ministers’ Meetings and National Standard Setting Bodies, including required content, process steps, consultation, analysis and OIA assessment expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for policy makers
rubrics_metrics.description: All governments will ensure that regulatory decisions will be consistent with the following principles:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy makers should clearly demonstrate a public policy problem necessitating government intervention, and should examine a range of genuine and viable options, including non‑regulatory options, to address the problem. Regulation should not be the default option: the policy option offering the greatest net benefit — regulatory or non-regulatory — should be the recommended option. Every major decision to regulate should be the subject of a Regulation Impact Statement. Policy makers should consult in a genuine and timely way with affected businesses, community organisations and individuals, as well as other policy makers to avoid creating cumulative or overlapping regulatory burdens. The information upon which policy makers base their decisions must be published at the earliest opportunity. All regulation should be periodically reviewed to test its continuing relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who the RIS is for — clarity, tone and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The RIS needs to be a factual and analytical assessment of the likely impacts and be targeted at decision‑makers, stakeholders and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RIS should be precise and economical in language, include only what is relevant, avoid unnecessary jargon and needlessly complex language, be measured and prudent in arguments, not pass off opinion as fact (check accuracy of every claim and say when facts are inconclusive), and be easy to navigate with clearly marked sections and logical flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIS as a two-stage process
rubrics_metrics.description: If regulatory options are being considered, decision‑making bodies must subject these options to the RIA process through a two‑stage process comprising a draft consultation RIS and a final decision RIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose of consultation RIS is to canvass options and elicit stakeholder information; purpose of decision RIS is to inform deliberations with conclusions on necessity and the most efficient/effective approach after consultation. Default requirement is both stages, but consultation RIS may be omitted where the consultation function has been achieved by an appropriate alternative mechanism (e.g. statutory consultation or prolonged ongoing consultation with demonstrable evidence). OIA has a template consultation RIS exemption letter agencies are encouraged to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIA assessment criteria for RISs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of Impact Analysis assesses RISs when requested by decision‑makers and provides independent advice on adequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIA will assess: the appropriateness of the type of analysis and whether the depth of analysis is commensurate with potential impacts; the rigour and transparency justifying any recommendation made in the RIS. The OIA aims to provide its assessment within two weeks of receipt of a draft consultation RIS or decision RIS.

rubrics_metrics.name: What needs to be included in a RIS
rubrics_metrics.description: A RIS must be a systematic examination of the costs and benefits of options for achieving an agreed policy objective or solution to an identified policy problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RIS must answer the seven RIS questions (see entries for each question) to a level of detail commensurate with the magnitude of the problem and potential impacts. There is flexibility in formatting but the requirement is to address the seven questions. Including an introductory/background section may be useful to outline purpose and context prior to the seven questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIS Question 1: What is the policy problem?
rubrics_metrics.description: The introductory section of the RIS must clearly identify and define the problem and demonstrate why it is a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must offer evidence about the magnitude of the problem and costs of doing nothing; describe the businesses, community organisations or individuals affected; identify existing legislation not being enforced; explain which current government measures have sought to address the problem and establish why those measures are not working. Consider market failure, regulatory failure, unacceptable hazard or risk; keep risk in perspective (identify underlying causes not symptoms); analyse likelihood versus consequences of risk; assess how the problem has been dealt with previously across jurisdictions and overseas and whether design or implementation is at fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIS Question 2: Why is government action needed?
rubrics_metrics.description: This section must clearly identify why there is a legitimate rationale for government intervention and demonstrate government capacity to intervene successfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify alternatives to government action, clearly state objectives/outcomes/goals/targets (objectives should be specific, measurable, accountable, realistic, timely), identify constraints or barriers, assess whether the problem is too small or the cost of intervention outweighs benefit, consider resource allocation inefficiencies, equity issues, monopoly or market power, information asymmetry, externalities, public goods, and behavioural ('irrational market') reasons for intervention. Doing nothing must be included as a benchmark option.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIS Question 3: What policy options are to be considered?
rubrics_metrics.description: The RIS must identify a range of genuine and viable alternative policy options and ensure live options can achieve the stated objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present clear, well‑differentiated options — a minimum of three options is required and the status quo must be posed as the benchmark. Do not present one option as a fait accompli. Consider mixes (different approaches for different groups), exemptions or lighter touch for small business, better enforcement of existing regulation, light‑touch/principles‑based regulation, self‑regulation, quasi‑regulation, co‑regulation, explicit government regulation, and a broad suite of alternative instruments (information/education, market‑based instruments, pre/post‑market schemes, bans/recalls, standards, service charters, audits, QA schemes). If standards differ from international standards, document why; consider trans‑Tasman alignment opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum options and benchmark requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every RIS must include a sufficient number of viable options and the status quo as a benchmark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The number of options should be commensurate with the magnitude of the problem but three is the minimum requirement. Non‑viable options should only be included if canvassed publicly. If the option with highest net benefit is not recommended, reasons must be transparent and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIS Question 4: What is the likely net benefit of each option? (cost–benefit and impact analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: This section must identify who is affected by each option and assess economic, competition, social, environmental and other costs and benefits, including distributional effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where relevant, quantify benefits and costs (including regulatory compliance costs) to a level commensurate with impact; analyse qualitative impacts; provide evidence, data sources and clearly identify assumptions. Consider business impacts (market intervention, paperwork, regulatory stipulations), community organisation impacts (service delivery, grant conditions), individual/household impacts (higher input costs, increased compliance effort), community/environment (employment, public health, environment), and government impacts (administration/enforcement costs). Include distributional analysis and competition considerations (incumbent businesses, market entry, sensitive markets). Use tools such as the Regulatory Burden Measurement framework where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIS Question 5: Who was consulted and how was their feedback incorporated?
rubrics_metrics.description: This section must explain the purpose and objectives of consultation, outline the consultation plan (for consultation RIS), and where consultation has occurred, summarise principal stakeholder views and how feedback affected the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate proper, genuine and timely consultation to understand affected parties' attitudes, ensure viable alternatives have been considered, confirm data accuracy, and identify implementation barriers and unintended consequences. List stakeholders consulted and summarise their views, areas of agreement and difference, and describe how proposals were modified or why dissenting views were not adopted. Use appropriate consultation tools; consultation should be continuous, broad‑based, accessible, not burdensome, transparent, consistent and flexible, subject to evaluation, and not rushed. Tailor channels to audience; consider social media, face‑to‑face, inbound calls, and accommodate resource constraints of small stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation characteristics and practical guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Best practice features of consultation processes for RISs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build consultative relationships continuously, capture diversity of stakeholders (including other governments and regulators), ensure accessibility and prompt responses, minimise burden (e.g. joint consultation), be transparent about objectives and decision context, evaluate consultation processes for relevance/effectiveness, and provide reasonable time for stakeholders to consider detailed information. Use OIA's Best Practice Consultation guidance note for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIS Question 6: What is the best option from those considered and how will it be implemented?
rubrics_metrics.description: This section must recommend a preferred option, explain what was learned from consultation, outline caveats, assumptions and unresolved issues, and discuss implementation arrangements and risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend the option taking into account costs and benefits (usually highest net benefit). Disclose and assess areas of uncertainty, methodological caveats, data limitations and assumptions. Cover implementation risks (likelihood, consequences, management), transitional arrangements, resourcing and governance, timeframes and project phases, and a plan for stakeholder engagement during implementation. Be explicit about how impacts are distributed and mitigation options. Convey information clearly to decision‑makers and make a confident recommendation that accounts for uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing an implementation plan
rubrics_metrics.description: An implementation plan must be included to deliver the proposed policy option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create shared understanding of objectives, expected outcomes and benefits, identify implementation challenges, timeframes, project phases, resourcing and governance arrangements, decision‑making authorities, and stakeholder engagement approaches. Identify risks, their likelihood and consequences, and mitigation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIS Question 7: How will the chosen option be evaluated?
rubrics_metrics.description: This section must describe how the policy's performance will be monitored and evaluated during and after implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an evaluation plan addressing implementation fidelity, effectiveness and efficiency in achieving intended outcomes, differential impacts on different groups, and plans for periodic review. Consider cumulative regulatory burden and ensure original objectives are maintained; schedule regular reviews to test continued relevance and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional analysis and competition considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: RISs must consider how costs and benefits are distributed across groups and any competition impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess distributional impacts (who bears costs/receives benefits), quantify significant distributional effects where possible, consider incumbent businesses and entry of new businesses, market sensitivity issues, effect on product quality/variety, consumer choice and switching costs, and whether the regulation will significantly alter competitiveness across sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidence, data and assumptions — transparency and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: All assessments should be based on evidence with data sources and assumptions clearly identified and limitations disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify where possible; analyse qualitative impacts where quantification is not feasible; disclose caveats about methodology, data quality and limitations and assess their potential effect on conclusions. When facts are inconclusive, say so. Ensure assumptions are explicit and tested (including through consultation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of international and trans‑Tasman standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The RIS should provide information on applicable international standards and whether the proposal differs from or adopts those standards, and consider opportunities for trans‑Tasman regulatory alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proposed standards differ from international standards, document why. Consider alignment with New Zealand where relevant to lower costs or deliver benefits to Australian and New Zealand businesses; where trans‑Tasman issues exist, consult the New Zealand Government and reflect its views in the RIS.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a consultation RIS may be exempted
rubrics_metrics.description: A consultation RIS may not be required where the consultation function has been achieved by an appropriate alternative mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumstances include statutory consultation inherent in the legislation/regulatory scheme or ongoing prolonged consultation where policy options have been tested with stakeholders and sufficient evidence exists to inform the decision RIS. Agencies are encouraged to use the OIA template consultation RIS exemption letter when seeking agreement that the consultation function has been met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external consultants
rubrics_metrics.description: External consultants may be engaged to help develop a RIS but agencies retain responsibility for content and must follow procurement rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultants are often best used for technical aspects (e.g. costings, cost‑benefit analysis) rather than drafting the whole RIS. Use procurement rules, ensure consultant engagement does not slow the RIS process. The OIA will not deal directly with consultants and will not provide feedback to them; the agency/secretariat remains responsible for ensuring the RIS addresses all seven questions and that analysis and consultation are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting an independent review of a RIS
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more jurisdictions may request an independent review of the proposed regulation if there is dissatisfaction with process or adequacy of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two Heads of Government write to the Chair of the decision‑making body to trigger an independent review. The decision‑making body nominates a review body to reassess whether the RIS was prepared in accordance with the Guide. The review re‑examines the assessment process (not necessarily repeat quantitative analysis) and reports publicly; jurisdictions requesting the review bear its cost. The decision‑making body retains discretion in how it uses the review and may still decide contrary to review recommendations.
